examples: I haven't done my homework yet.
It hasn't started raining yet.
I'm not going yet.
There's no present yet.
He isn't a student yet.
A: Have you eaten yet? B: No, not yet.
fields.explain:
Formal: use まだ～ません／まだ～ていません in polite conversation.
Nuance difference:まだ行きません: not going "at this moment".まだ行っていません: up to now "still haven't gone (even once/haven't started)".
まだ行きません: not going "at this moment".
まだ行っていません: up to now "still haven't gone (even once/haven't started)".
Emphasis: まだ + は is used to highlight the topic being contrasted (例:宿題はまだです)。
With time expressions: まだ＋今／今日／この週… emphasizes the sense of "it's not time yet".

Core meaning: まだ indicates that a situation "still" remains unchanged; with the negative (～ません／～ない／～ていません) it means "not yet, still not, has not happened/been completed".
まだ + Vません: emphasizes not-yet at present, implying a decision or schedule: "not doing it right now".
まだ + Vていません: emphasizes the state up to the time of speaking, "still haven't done it/it still hasn't happened", suitable for expressing experience/result.
まだ + N は/が ありません: "there is no N yet". まだ + Aく/では ありません: "not yet (reached the level/state)".
Implied expectation: usually implies that the action will happen in the future (unlike "never").
fields.notes:
In casual speech, ～ません ⇄ ～ない: まだ行かない／まだ食べてない.
With verbs of experience: まだ行ったことがありません "have never been there yet".
With quantities: まだ三枚あります "there are still 3 sheets". In the negative: まだ三枚もありません "there aren't even 3 sheets yet".
mistakes: Using まだ～ません to express the state of "never having done" → まだ～ていません/～たことがありません is more natural.
Confusing まだあります (still have) with まだありません (don't have yet).
Mixing up まだ and もう: もう～ません = no longer… (unlike まだ～ません = not yet).
Past tense with まだ: avoid まだ行きました (contradictory). Use まだ行っていません or もう行きました.

rows: More natural for saying "haven't done it" up to now
まだ<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べていません

— もう<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった？ — いいえ、まだです。

examples: The train will be here soon.
It's almost three o'clock.
Spring is almost here.
It's going to rain soon.
Yamada will arrive soon.
A: When are we leaving? B: We're leaving soon.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a sense of "imminence": used when the wait is not long.
In formal announcements, まもなく is more appropriate; もうすぐ leans toward conversation.
Can be used with natural phenomena, schedules, and states that are about to change.

Meaning: Expresses something that will happen in the near future, with a sense of "almost there/about to happen".
Casual, neutral nuance; can be used in everyday conversation.
Does not express the past; used with the present/near future or N + です.
fields.notes:
With potential/plan verbs: もうすぐ行けます (will soon be able to go).
Exclamation: もうすぐだ！ (Almost there!).
In descriptive written language: もうすぐ町が見えてくる (The town will soon come into view).
mistakes: Using the past with もうすぐ: × もうすぐ行った → ✓ もうすぐ行きます。
A direct negative is unnatural: × もうすぐ行きません → Say “まだ行きません” (not going yet) or use another expression that fits the context.
Confusing "already" with "soon": もう春です (it's already spring) ≠ もうすぐ春です (spring is almost here).
Confusing degrees of "nearness": すぐ (immediately) is stronger than もうすぐ (soon, not instant).

fields.connection: もう + Vた (already…) / もう + Vない (no longer…)
examples: I've already eaten.
Have you done your homework yet?
I'm not going anymore.
There's no more cake.
Once more, please.
Please speak a little more slowly.
fields.explain:
Strong affirmative "already done": もう + Vた emphasizes completion.
Definite stop: もう + Vない／Vません shows a decision "not to do it anymore".
Polite: the short reply もういいです (that's enough/no longer needed) in service and shopping.
Casual: もう行った？／もうやらない。

Meaning 1: "already" with the past/completion (happened before the time of speaking).
Meaning 2: "no longer…" with the negative, showing the end of a habit/intention.
Meaning 3: "more, another" in quantity phrases (もう一度: once more; もう少し: a little more).
Implied expectation: a question with もう usually implies the asker thinks it may have already happened.
fields.notes:
In yes/no answers:
A: もう食べましたか。 B: はい、もう食べました／いいえ、まだです。
A: もう食べましたか。 B: はい、もう食べました／いいえ、まだです。
もう + non-past present can still mean "right now/soon" in spoken language: もう行くね (I'm off now).
Negative of existence: もうNがない = "there is no more N".
mistakes: Confusing もう～ません (no longer…) with まだ～ません (not yet). The meanings are opposite.
Using もう with the present in the wrong context: “もう行きます” is fine (I'm off/going right now), but it does not mean "already" in the past sense.
Answering “もうです” is unnatural. Use “はい、もうしました／いいえ、まだです”。
Confusing もうすぐ (soon) with もう (already). Example: もう春です (it's already spring) vs もうすぐ春です (spring is almost here).

rows: Completed before the time of speaking
すでに<ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>した

fields.connection: もっと + A/Na / もっと + [Adverb] + V
examples: Please speak a little more slowly.
This book is interesting. I want to read more.
It's cold today. I hear it will be even colder tomorrow.
Let's study more before the test.
Next time, please sing in a louder voice.
For your health, you should eat more vegetables.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes an increase: placed right before the word being intensified (A/V/Adv).
Polite: combine with 〜てください／ましょう to soften it. A direct “もっと！” can sound strong.
“もう少し” is milder than “もっと”: もう少し＝a little more; もっと＝considerably more.
With specific quantities: usually “もう＋[number＋counter]”（もう一杯）; “もっと” leans toward general degree (もっと多く).

Core meaning: "more, even more; increasing the degree/amount/speed… compared with now/expectations".
Used to:
Request/advise an increase in degree: もっと静かに、もっと頑張って。
Express a desire: もっと日本語が話せるようになりたい。
Make a progressive comparison:今年は去年よりもっと忙しい。
Request/advise an increase in degree: もっと静かに、もっと頑張って。
Express a desire: もっと日本語が話せるようになりたい。
Make a progressive comparison:今年は去年よりもっと忙しい。
Nuance: the speaker feels something is "not enough/lacking" and wants to "increase" it.
Position: comes before the adjective/adverb/verb it emphasizes.
fields.notes:
In conversation, “もっと！” can be used on its own as a command/encouragement.
With Aな: change it to Aに (きれいに、上手に) when it modifies a verb: もっときれいに書いて。
“もっと多くのN” (written language): もっと多くの人, but conversation usually uses “もっと人が…/人をもっと…”.
Combined with advice: もっと〜たほうがいい (You should ~ more).
mistakes: Using it directly before a noun: ✕ もっと日本語→ instead:日本語をもっと勉強する／もっと日本語が話したい.
Confusing it with “もう”: “もう三枚ください”（3 more sheets） is more natural than “もっと三枚ください”.
Wrong superlative combination: ✕ もっと一番速い → いちばん速い（the most）／もっと速い（more）.
Confusing it with “もっとも”: もっと（more） ≠ もっとも（the most / however).

examples: I often go to the park on weekends.
I often listen to Japanese music.
He can speak Japanese well.
Sorry, I couldn't hear your name well.
When I was a child, I often played with my friends.
This movie is well made.
fields.explain:
Position: comes before the verb and modifies the whole action.
With the negative: expresses "not clearly/not well": よくわかりません； for negative frequency, use あまり〜ません.
Slight differences: よく vs たびたび（more formal）; よく vs いつも（always, higher frequency）.

Meaning 1 (N5): frequency "often, frequently". Example: よく行きます（I often go）.
Meaning 2 (N5): degree of quality "well/clearly enough/skillfully". Example: よくわかります（I understand well）.
With the negative: よくわかりません＝"don't understand well", not "don't often understand". To say "not often", use あまり〜ません.
Context determines the meaning: よく飲む（drink often） vs よくできた（well done）.
fields.notes:
The kanji良く is sometimes seen in written language, but hiragana よく is common at N5.
Emphatic intonation can change the nuance: よくやった！（Well done!）.
よくも（N3~）carries a nuance of reproach: よくもそんなことを…（How dare you…）— not part of basic N5.
mistakes: Using よく＋Vません to say "not often": ✕ よく行きません → 〇 あまり行きません.
Confusing よく with上手に:日本語がよく話せます（natural）;日本語が上手に話せます (OK, but emphasizes "skillfully").
Using it with adjectives of degree: ✕ よく暑い → 〇 とても暑い／よく暑くなります（often gets hot）.
Misunderstanding the meaning: よくわかりません＝don't understand well; not "rarely understand".

fields.explain:
Adding か after a question word gives a word meaning "some + question word": for example, なに is "what", so なにか is "something".
The particles へ,を after question word + か can be omitted.

examples: Harada understands English.
I don't understand anything at all.
My house is between the bookstore and the park.

fields.explain:
Distinguish知る (come to know) vs知っている (know);結婚する (get married) vs結婚している (be married, a state).
Vてある vs Vている: てある emphasizes an intentional result with transitive verbs; ている is neutral/a natural state, or is used with intransitive verbs.
With着る/はく/かぶる... + ている, it expresses "be wearing/have on".
The contracted spoken forms ～てる/～でる are common, but are not used in formal written language.

Progressive: an action at the time of speaking (今勉強しています).
Habit/repeated action: describes regular activities (毎日日本語を勉強しています).
A current state created by a previous action: ドアが開いています (the door is open),結婚しています (got married and is now in that state).
Verbs of perception/knowledge:知っています（know）、知りません（don't know) → use ている to indicate the state of knowing/not knowing.
With verbs of motion:行っています can mean "is going" (with今/これから) or "goes regularly/has gone and is there now", depending on context.
fields.notes:
Choose the correct intransitive/transitive verb:窓が開いている（intransitive verb）vs窓を開けている（in the act of opening, a different meaning).
持っている can mean holding/owning; distinguish by context:今チケットを持っている（have it in hand now）.
With instantaneous verbs of change (死ぬ、壊れる…), ている usually indicates the state after the change:彼は死んでいる。
mistakes: Wrong transitive/intransitive verb: ×窓を開いています → ◯窓が開いています /窓を開けています (different meaning).
Confusing知る and知っている: ×彼を知ります → ◯彼を知っています.
Misunderstanding行っている: it can mean "is going/goes regularly/has gone and is there", depending on context.
JLPT: identify the three uses (progressive, habit, state) from context; distinguish ている and てある.

examples: I brush my teeth after eating.
I go to work after eating breakfast.
Since coming to Japan, I've come to like sushi.
I'll call you after I finish work.
Please play after you've done your homework.
You can't enter the kitchen until you've washed your hands.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes completion: V1 must finish before V2; suitable for instructions/procedures.
"Right after": add すぐ/すぐに to make the immediacy clear.
In the meaning "ever since", it often goes with それ以来／ずっと to emphasize duration.
Not used to give a reason with a direct command; if you need a reason + request, use ので／から.

Indicates a clear time order: V1 is completed before V2 is done; different from simple listing with ～て.
Used as a time reference point, "ever since": Vてから、ずっと～ (continuously until now).
The negative variants emphasize a prerequisite: ～てからでないと／～てからでなければ.
Usually has the same subject when it is a sequence of one person's actions; with different subjects, it mainly shows the time relationship and does not emphasize cause.
fields.notes:
In procedures/instruction signs, ～てから sounds polite but clear: “カードを入れてから、暗証番号を押してください”。
In the meaning "ever since", it often goes with a change of state: ～てから、～ようになった／～くなった.
No second “から” is needed: a single “から” after Vて is enough.
mistakes: Confusing it with後で: ×宿題をして後で遊ぶ (sounds disjointed) → ◯宿題をしてから遊ぶ.
Using it for cause: ×雨が降ってから、中止した (emphasizes cause) → use降ったので／から中止した instead.
Different subjects cause ambiguity: prefer the same subject when it is a sequence of personal actions.
JLPT: often tests ～てからでないと／～てからでなければ and the "right after" nuance with すぐ.

examples: Please write your name here.
Please speak slowly.
Please don't take pictures.
Could you please say that once more?
Could you open the window for me?
Please check.
fields.explain:
Used directly toward the listener; with superiors/customers, prefer ～ていただけますか／～てくださいませんか to be more polite.
Add softening openers: すみませんが／恐れ入りますが／よろしければ + ～てください。
The negative uses ないでください (not なくてください).
In instructions/procedures, ～てください is used in sequence: カードを入れてください。次に、暗証番号を押してください。

Makes a polite request or suggestion for the listener to do action V.
The negative “～ないでください” is used to forbid/ask someone not to do something with moderate politeness.
Politeness increases: ～て → ～てください → ～てくださいませんか／～ていただけますか.
In service language/signs, the form お／ご～ください is concise, very polite and formal.
fields.notes:
In business emails, the form お／ご～ください is very common: ご返信ください／ご確認ください.
“ください” also means "please give me" with nouns:水をください (outside the scope of Vてください, but common).
Chaining requests: ～て、～てください for coherence; avoid too many consecutive commands, which sounds stiff.
mistakes: Wrong negative: ×来なくてください → ◯来ないでください.
Being too direct with superiors: replace it with ～ていただけますか／～てくださいませんか.
Dropping て: ×窓を開けください → ◯窓を開けてください.
JLPT: distinguish the politeness levels of ください／くれますか／いただけますか; recognize お／ご～ください as standard keigo.

fields.meaning: A way of giving someone permission to carry out an action (expressed with a volitional verb).
examples: Do not throw garbage outside.
Do not feed the animals.
We must not forget the war.
You must not mention that in front of her.

A: You can't use your phone here.
B: Okay. I'm very sorry.
fields.explain: Prohibition: not allowing someone to do an action.

fields.meaning:
it's OK to ~.
it's all right to ~.
fields.connection: Vて + もいい(です) / N + で / Na + で / Aい + い くて / Vても + いいですか・かまいませんか（question asking for permission）
examples:
A: Excuse me, may I smoke?
B: Yes, go ahead.

A: Excuse me, may I play the guitar?
B: Sure, that's fine.
fields.explain:
Asking for or giving permission to do an action.
When not giving permission, answer tactfully with すみません、ちょっと…, or answer with a prohibition using the いけません structure in the next grammar point.

examples: Please don't come in here.
Please don't press this button.
Please don't interrupt me.
Please don't watch TV late at night.
Please don't cry.
Don't push yourself too hard.
fields.explain:
Polite and gentler than “～な！” (harsh command).
Often used on signs, in instructions, or when you want to ask someone to avoid doing something.
In casual speech, it can be contracted to ～ないでね or ～ないで .
例：そんなこと言わ ないでね。→ Don't say that, okay?
Not used with nouns or adjectives – only with verbs .

Expresses a polite request or suggestion for someone not to do an action.
It is the negative form of ～てください(please do…), meaning "please don't…".
The speaker uses it to give a gentle command or a polite reminder in conversation, instructions, or rules.
Mainly used with listeners of equal or lower status (such as friends, students, customers…).
fields.notes:
In notices and public signs, you often see the forms:～しないでくださいor～は禁止です(is prohibited).
To say it more gently, you can use:～ないようにしてください（Please try not to…）.
At JLPT N5, this is the basic pattern for expressing a polite negative request.
mistakes: Wrong conjugation of the nai-form:話す →話さないでください(correct),話しないでください(incorrect).
Confusing it with the imperative form “～な！” (rude, impolite).
Forgetting 「で」: ✕行かないください → ○行かないでください.
JLPT N5 often tests: choosing the correct polite negative request structure between ～てください and ～ないでください.

rows: ここに<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ってください。
Request not to do an action
ここに<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>らないでください。
